He wakes with a headache and a strange flatness, and there is nobody in his head who was not there two years ago.

He watches the ugliest rooms lose their walls first. The shouting, the silences, the door — gone in the order he'd rather forget them, which should be a mercy and isn't. Two technicians work the machine from his flat while he sleeps under the cap; one of them, a wiry man named Peck, quietly slides a bagged hairslide and a torn page into his own coat, keeping for himself everything that once made a woman love somebody.

Tobias gets to the platform for work and gets on the other train instead, and cannot say why. He walks out onto frozen sand and finds a woman with dyed hair already standing on it.

Inside the dissolving rooms he reaches the ones he wants to keep and starts to run, carrying her out of her own memories and into places she was never in — a childhood kitchen, under a table, anywhere the map doesn't reach. He has changed his mind and there is no one to tell.

They drive back into the city talking too easily for strangers, and outside her building she asks him up for a drink as though it were the second time.

On the outside, Dell and Rosa are drinking his beer and dancing on his bed in their underwear when the map on the screen stops corresponding to anything, and neither of them notices for a long time.

Two envelopes arrive on the same morning. They sit in her stairwell listening to their own voices give the reasons it ended, and she runs, and comes back up, and they decide to do it anyway.

Dr. Hallam is called out at three a.m. to put the erasure back on its rails. In the hallway Rosa kisses him, and his wife, arriving behind her, tells her exactly why she has always felt that way about him and cannot remember why.

At the end of the rail line, on a cold beach full of strangers, a man with nothing to say to anyone ends up talking to a woman with dyed hair. They break the window of a shuttered house on the shore and sleep on the boards.

The last thing left in him is that same house. In the doorway of a room already going, Ivy tells him to walk out, and then to come and find her at the coast.

Two years pass in small rooms and cold weather — the ice of a frozen river, steam on a noodle-house window, the back seat of a drive-in with the sound turned down. He is happy in a way he cannot describe to anyone; she has found somewhere she can stop moving.

Rosa empties the filing cabinets on her way out of the clinic and posts every patient their own file — the forms, the object lists, the tape of the session where they explained what they wanted taken out.

The same rooms turn against them. She drinks and he counts it; he says nothing and she calls it contempt. Each of them has learned exactly which sentence does the most damage.

He fills two carrier bags with everything that has her in it — a hairslide, a mug, a torn page — so the clinic can find what memories they're pinned to.

She comes in at two in the morning having put his car into something on the way, and the argument that starts over the dent finishes somewhere neither of them can come back from. She takes a bag and goes.

Two friends hand him the form letter the clinic sent to everyone she knew. He carries it straight to the director's office and asks to be given the same thing, that afternoon if possible.

She takes herself to a clinic in a shabby office building and pays to have a man taken out of her head — every room, every argument, every good afternoon — as though he had never been in it.

He goes to the bookshop to make it up with her and she looks at him the way you look at a customer. There's a young man behind the counter, laughing at everything he says, and she does not know who Tobias is at all.

And now, on the stairwell floor, with both tapes gone quiet, they know exactly how it goes: the good middle, the curdling, the door. They know it and they climb the last flight together anyway.

Martin sits on the end of a motel bed he cannot remember taking and tells a stranger on the telephone about Elias Prine, the man with no new memories, the wife who tested him with injection after injection until she was dead of trust. The voice on the other end asks patient questions. Martin doesn't know why he keeps telling this story. He only knows he denied that claim once, from behind a desk, certain the mind was doing it to itself.

Two men came through his bathroom door at night. He shot one across his wife's body; the other put his head into the mirror, and since then nothing new has stayed. He built himself out of paper after that — instant photographs, block capitals, five facts cut into his thigh where he couldn't lose them. A plainclothes officer named Roy found the second man for him, out past the edge of town, and stood by while Martin finished it. Within minutes Martin was asking who they'd been looking for.

On the telephone now, the caller gives him a name: Gil Marsh, a dealer, an address. Martin writes it down as fact. In a basement with water on the floor he beats a man half his weight and holds a belt to his throat until it's over, and photographs what's left. The dying man whispers a word — *Elias* — that means nothing to him. He puts on the dead man's suit and drives his car away.

Roy is waiting when he leaves the building. He sits Martin down and tells him plainly: the dealer was nobody, the revenge already happened a year ago, and the case he keeps reciting to strangers isn't a case at all — it's his own house, his own wife, his own hands. Martin cannot hold a truth that would leave him nothing. He burns the photographs of Gil, writes *he is lying to you* across Roy's picture, and copies the plate off the car outside as the next thing he will be certain of. He carries the note into a parlour and has it inked under the five facts already on his leg, not remembering writing it.

Behind her bar, Corinne watches a stranger walk in wearing a suit she knows, driving a car she knows, and has the staff spit in his beer before it reaches him. She clears every pen from her house before he arrives. She goads him until he swings, waits outside for the bruises to rise, comes back in and blames a man named Vance. Martin, certain of nothing but what's written, waits in a motel bathroom in the dark and takes Vance down as he comes through, drives him out to the edge of town at gunpoint with a warning he will never remember giving.

Weeks earlier, in the field, Martin burned a hairbrush and a paperback, trying to finish a grief that will not stay finished in him. He fed the fire and waited to feel the end of something and felt only the fire.

Corinne runs the plate through a friend at the registry and lays the printout in his hand: Roy Mercer. Martin reads it as though for the first time, because for him it is. He lures Roy back to the derelict building on a pretext, walks him into the room, and puts one through his head, and photographs the body, satisfied that the note was right.

On the telephone, still, in the room he cannot remember taking, Martin tells the story of Elias Prine again — the wife, the injections, the memory that would not hold — to a caller who already seems to know how it ends, who lets him finish, who never once tells him whose story it really is.

The warehouse smelled of oil and cordite and, underneath it, petrol. Mr. Elm lay on the ramp with his shirt gone dark and Ash's hands pressed into the wound like he could hold the blood inside by will alone. "Nobody dies here today," Ash kept saying, as though saying it enough would make it a rule of the building.

It hadn't started here. It had started in an empty room with Pruitt walking him through a story about a bag of drugs and four dogs in a public lavatory, over and over, until Danny stopped reciting it and started remembering it as if it were his own bad night. He'd told it to men who'd heard every kind of liar — Bram, Cal, Ash — and gotten the laugh in the right place, and walked out with a job and a colour-free name he hadn't picked.

Ren had walked into that same office off the back of a long sentence he could have shortened by talking, and Bram had handed him an envelope and a place on the job for his silence. At breakfast, eight men in black suits had argued about what a pop song really meant and whether the waitress had earned an extra dollar for the coffee. Nobody used a real name. Later, in the office, Bram dealt out tree names off a list so no one could give up anyone else, and Birch spent a full minute complaining that his was the worst of them.

Then it had gone wrong inside a minute. The alarm already running, Ash firing through the windscreen and both side windows as the car went the wrong way down the wrong street. Danny had run until he had no more running in him, dragged a woman out of her own car, and she'd put a bullet in his stomach from the pocket pistol before he could shut the door. He'd shot her and driven himself bleeding to the rendezvous, screaming the whole way, until Ash carried him in and swore, kneeling in the blood, that this wasn't going to be how it ended.

Birch arrived clean and furious, walked them through the timings, said the police had been on the pavement before the first alarm went up, and went out to hide the diamonds where no one watching him could see. Someone inside this room had called it in. Nobody said the word informer, but it sat in the air with the petrol smell.

Ren came in late, unhurried, complained about the shouting, then opened his boot and dragged out a young patrolman named Doyle with his hands tied behind him. Left alone with him, Ren found an oldies station on the radio, danced a few steps, took the man's ear off with a razor, and poured a can of petrol over him for the pleasure of watching him understand what was coming.

Danny, from the floor, with nothing left in him but the one thing that mattered, emptied his gun into Ren before the lighter came down. Then he told Doyle what he was — a police officer — and that there were cars in the street waiting for Bram to walk into them.

Cal came back to a body and a story, listened, decided it held, and put three rounds into Doyle himself to close it clean.

Bram arrived last. He looked at the man on the floor a long moment and said, flatly, that this was the one. Ash put his gun on Bram instead and would not be told otherwise — the man he'd carried in his arms was his, whatever else he was.

Three guns came up in a room the size of a garage, and all three went off. When it stopped, only Ash and Danny were still making a noise.

Bleeding out beside him, Danny said it plainly, because Ash had earned the truth. Ash dragged himself upright, put the gun to his own head, and the doors came in as he fired — cut down where he knelt, in the last second of believing he'd been right to trust him.

There is a heart, and it does not know whose chest it is in. That is the only fact that holds still in this telling; everything else moves depending on where you stand to look at it.

Aaron hears the pistol before he remembers buying it. He is behind a motel in the dark with a man against a wall who he has never met, and his hand will not close the way he wants it to, and the shot goes somewhere that will not kill, and he is telling a stranger to get up and run before he understands that the stranger is the reason his own chest still moves at all.

Before that, or after — it hardly matters which word you use for it — a woman sits at a kitchen table with the girls' drawings still taped to the wall behind her, and does in the bathroom what she used to do in the bathroom, years ago, before the fixed-rate mortgage and the school run and the husband who adored her. She says she cannot go on breathing in the same country as a man she has never met, and she keeps saying it until the saying becomes a plan, and the plan becomes a gun under a car seat.

Elsewhere a boy's baseball coach with scripture on both forearms testifies to anyone who will sit still, and his wife watches the certainty in him the way you watch weather. He is one shock away from something; nobody can say what, least of all him. And in another room, in a season that might come before or after any of this, a mathematician is shown numbers on a screen and told that weeks are all that are left to him, and his estranged wife presses a clinic form across the table and asks him to sign while he still can.

The pickup comes through the crossing. This much is fixed, though nothing around it is: a man and two children taken off their feet, an engine idling a hundred yards on, a truck backing up and then going. A widow is told in a corridor, first about her husband and then, while she is still absorbing the first sentence, about both girls. A chest is opened in the same building and a heart that was beating an hour ago in somebody else is put into it, and a man who has not breathed easily in months lies awake at night listening to it going.

He cannot stop thinking about whose it was. A man in a car park takes his money and hands him a name and a street, against every rule there is. He learns which pool she swims at and arranges to be in the water until it stops looking like chance, and within a fortnight he is in her house, not telling her the one thing that matters. When he finally says it, badly, in her kitchen, she puts him out with everything he brought, and four days later takes him back knowing exactly what he's carrying.

He tells his wife he is not coming back, that he does not want the child she wanted made from what was left in the freezer, and she tells him the truth of it — that he is spending a life somebody else paid for.

The man who confessed at a police station and went back inside is released early on someone's recommendation, gets as far as the gate, looks at the family waiting, and keeps walking anyway, out to a motel four hundred miles from any of it, cleaning rooms for a wage.

He follows the two of them back to their own door that night, bleeding through his shirt, and asks to be finished. The man who could not pull the trigger the first time turns the gun around instead and puts it into his own chest, into the borrowed muscle, as if returning it.

They get him into a car with the horn down, and on the table the heart stops for good, the same one that started this, going back into the ground it came out of. The man who walked away from his family goes home to it. The woman who wanted him dead goes home alone, carrying something she did not expect to be carrying, and nobody left to tell her when any of it happened, or in what order, or why.

The nurse said he woke once more before the end, and that the word he said was not a name anyone in the house recognized. Nobody had thought to ask him earlier what it meant, and now there was no one left to ask.

The newsreel ran nine minutes in a warm little screening room full of men with notebooks, and it went from the boarding house to the banker to the fortune to the Clarion to the palace on the hill without once explaining why any of it had happened, or why it had ended the way it did, alone, in an unfinished house, with a word on his lips that meant nothing to the reporters watching. Nash was sent to find out what the word meant. He started with the second wife because she seemed the likeliest to know and the least likely to lie kindly. She was drunk at four in the afternoon in a seaside club, and she told him to get out before he had finished asking.

So he went looking elsewhere, and the looking took him backward, the way looking always does.

He read the banker Barrow's memoir first, in which a boy on a mining claim in the west was signed over to a stranger at his mother's kitchen table the week his family got rich, the father objecting uselessly from the doorway. The boy had put a sled into Barrow's stomach hard enough to sit him down before they took him east anyway, and Barrow wrote about it fondly, as though the boy had done him credit.

The rest came from people, not paper. Marsh told him about the morning the fortune came due, when Emmett Rusk, twenty-five years old and richer than sense allowed, had looked down the list of his own holdings and asked for the newspaper nobody wanted, because he thought it might be fun. He'd moved a cot into the office, put Marsh on one side of him and a friend named Devlin on the other, and printed his principles on the front page over his own signature. Then he'd hired away the whole staff of the paper across the street and thrown them a party with a brass band, dancing in the middle of it himself.

Devlin, when Nash found him in another city working a smaller desk, told the rest without much bitterness left in it. The wedding to Adele, the governor's niece, splashed across every front page but Emmett's own. The breakfasts that got quieter and the table that got longer until husband and wife sat at either end of it reading rival papers. Then the shopgirl with mud-flecked toothache and a laugh that cost nothing, and the secret rooms, and the party boss Halloran marching the wife up the stairs ten days before the election to make his trade — withdraw, or be ruined by Monday — and being thrown out for his trouble. The election lost anyway, in six columns of FRAUD AT THE POLLS, and Devlin asking for a transfer, and the marriage going quietly while nobody watched.

Then the second marriage, forced onto a stage she had no voice for, and Devlin's own drunken half-review finished in Emmett's colder hand and printed and signed and the firing that came with it. The poison she swallowed rather than sing again. The permission, finally, to stop. And then Silvermount — the palace with ceilings too high to heat, where she did jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a hall built for a hundred people who never came, until a joyless picnic on a black beach ended in a quarrel and she packed her bags and went, and he could only tell her, uselessly, that she couldn't.

Colm the butler was the one who told him about the globe — how the old man had torn the abandoned bedroom apart with his own hands and stopped over a glass ball full of snow, said one word to no one, and carried it past the long mirrors that gave him back smaller and smaller until he disappeared into himself.

Nash closed his notebook in the marble library at Silvermount, having found the word but not what it weighed, and told himself no single word explains a life. Below him, in the yard, workmen were shoveling the crates out of the great hall, and among them, unremarked, a child's sled marked BLUEBELL went into the furnace with everything else.

THE WATCH

The boy sat very still while the veteran, still smelling of transit and other men's cigarettes, put the gold watch into his hands. "Your father carried this the whole time," the man said. "Kept it hidden through everything. Wanted you to have it." Denny turned it over and over, the metal warm from being carried so long against another man's ribs.

Years later, in a motel room on the edge of a city he could not go back to, Denny asked Marielle if she'd packed it.

She hadn't. It was still on the bedside table in a flat that was certainly being watched.

"It's just a watch," she said.

"It's not," he said, and that was the end of the conversation.

He went back for it anyway, let himself in quiet, found it exactly where it had been left. He was at the kitchen counter, the watch already warm in his palm, when a man came out of the bathroom he hadn't checked, and the submachine gun on the counter was nearer to Denny's hand than the man's gun was to his. Afterward there was a body in the doorway and the watch was back where it belonged, on his wrist, and it stayed there through the crash in the street, through the basement, through the moment he put down the sword instead of leaving with it, through the ride out of the city with Marielle's arms around his waist and the road going gray and straight ahead of them.

That was one thread through Denny's life, the watch. Here is the other, tangled through everyone around him.

Rollo and Marcus argued in the car about what a hamburger was called abroad, and about drug laws, and never once mentioned the man they were about to kill. In the corridor outside the flat they argued about whether a foot massage was worth being thrown off a balcony for. Then Marcus recited a line of scripture at Tobin and they shot him and took the briefcase, and a fourth man came out of the bathroom nobody had checked and unloaded a revolver at them from six feet and hit nothing. Marcus stood in front of the bullet holes and called it a miracle.

In the car after, Rollo's gun went off over some remark and took off the head of the man in the back seat. Marcus drove the ruined car to Warren's garage, where a soft-spoken fixer hosed them down in borrowed light and dressed them in shorts and T-shirts while he timed the work to the minute.

That was why, later that morning, two men in borrowed clothes carried a briefcase into a coffee shop and sat down to eat, right as a couple in the next booth decided nobody ever robs a restaurant and stood up on the seats with a pistol out. Marcus handed over his own wallet, recited his line again, told the frightened boy what he'd decided it meant, and let them walk. He kept the briefcase.

They delivered it, still in borrowed clothes, to Otis's bar, where Otis was counting money into an aging boxer's hand and telling him which round to take the fall in. That boxer was Denny.

Rollo went out that night to Kip's for heroin, pure enough to notice, and shot up at the kitchen table. Then he took Otis's wife Nadia dancing at a themed diner, and they won the contest barefoot, and back at the flat she found the bag in his coat and thought it was something else and nearly died on the carpet before Kip drove a needle into her heart.

Denny did not go down in the fifth. He won, and the other man never got up, and Denny was in a taxi before the crowd understood what they'd watched. Otis's money was gone and so was his patience — which was how Rollo ended up waiting in Denny's bathroom with a gun.

Driving away afterward, Denny found Otis crossing the street in front of his car with a paper bag in his arms, and put the car through him. Both wrecked; both were dragged into a pawnshop basement. Denny got loose, was nearly to the door, and turned back for a sword off the wall instead of leaving. Otis told him after that they were square, so long as he never came back.

So Denny collected Marielle, took a motorcycle from the shop, and rode out with the watch on his wrist, warm again, carried the way it had always been carried — hidden, then given, then nearly lost, then kept.

I hadn't slept in six months when I found out that a folding chair in a church basement, surrounded by strangers with real diseases, could put me under for a full night if I cried hard enough and let one of them hold me. Four evenings a week I went and grieved for cancers and blood conditions that weren't mine, and it worked, right up until the night a woman named Ada showed up smoking through the meditation, obviously faking, and I recognized the fake because it was mine. After that I didn't sleep again for a long time.

On a night flight not long before, I'd sat next to a soap salesman named Rex Marrow who talked for forty minutes about how everything either of us owned had been picked out for us by other people, and I kept his card because I didn't know what else to do with a man like that.

I want to tell you what happens at the end, because you'll need it later. There is a stairwell in a tower made of debt records, and a man walks me down it a flight at a time, hitting me, and at the bottom I understand the gun in his hand is in mine. I put it in my mouth and fire through my cheek. That is where this goes.

But first: my flat went up in an explosion while I was traveling, every catalogue thing I owned on the pavement, and I called Rex instead of anyone sane and he took me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district with no working plumbing. Outside a bar not long after, he asked me to hit him as hard as I could, and we beat each other bloody in the car park and laughed doing it. That became a Saturday. That became a cellar with rules read aloud. That became a waiting list.

Ada overdosed and called, and it was Rex who went and brought her back to the house, and the two of them kept me awake through the floorboards for weeks while I lay there rigid, unable to say why it mattered so much.

Rex was rendering fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into soap on the kitchen stove, selling it back to the department stores the women had shopped in before they were cut. He held my hand flat on that same table once and poured lye on the back of it and wouldn't let me leave my body to survive it. I still have the mark.

I walked into my employer's office and asked to be paid to disappear, and when he said no I beat my own face into his carpet until security found us both. He paid.

The cellar became an organization Rex called Havoc — shaved heads, sleeping on floors, going out at night to break things that belonged to companies. I couldn't say when it stopped being mine.

He drove a car into oncoming traffic once, let it roll, asked the men in back what they wished they'd done, and when I woke in the ditch he wasn't there and wasn't anywhere.

A boy named Ogden was shot dead coming out of a job with a drill still in his hand, and I started trying to tear down the thing I'd built.

I went city to city trying to stop it and found the same cellar everywhere, the same rules on the same wall, and men who looked up and called me Rex Marrow like it was simply my name.

In a motel room with the flight records spread over the bed it went together — one body, one account, one man awake and one man asleep, and every conversation between us held in an empty room. I called Ada and asked whose bed she'd been in. Mine, obviously, she said. What's wrong with you.

I found the vans under the towers, wired and timed, and understood at last what all of it had been for.

Which brings us back to the stairwell, the gun, my own hand.

The shaved men brought her to me afterward, apologized, and left. We stood at the window with my face wrapped and held hands while the towers went down in order, one after another, exactly as planned.

Nadir stood at the counter with Sahar beside him, translating even the parts he understood, while the dealer behind the glass did an impression of his accent for the benefit of nobody in particular. He bought the gun anyway. He had been broken into twice, he said, and Sahar said it again in the flatter voice she used for other people's ears.

What none of them knew yet — what would only make sense afterward, on a porch, in the dark, with a child running toward him — was that Sahar had gone back alone the next day and quietly asked for the box that does nothing.

Trey and Kwame took the prosecutor's car outside a restaurant, joking about who was watching them right up until the guns came out. Halstead stood very still. His wife, Paula, stood very still too, and then went home and stood at the top of her own stairs telling her husband, at a volume meant for the man fitting their new locks, that the tattooed one would be selling their keys to his friends by morning. Mateo said nothing. He finished the lock and left.

Boyle pulled the Hobarts over for nothing at all, put Renee on the hood of the car, and searched her with his hand where it had no business going while Clay stood three feet away and said nothing. Voss, watching, went to his commander the next morning and said he couldn't ride with the man anymore. He got a new car by calling it flatulence and telling himself that settled something.

Mateo went to Nadir's shop to fit a new lock and told him the door itself was rotten. Nadir heard a man inventing a second job for himself and threw him out. The door came off its hinges that same week, in the dark, and the insurer read the file and declined, citing the warning he'd refused.

Boyle sat across a desk from a clerk named Delia Frank and begged for a referral for his father, and got a flat no, and lost his temper at her badge. It would be easy to say that explained him. It explained nothing, and excused less. Not long after, he was the one who crawled into an overturned wreck with fuel running toward the flame and got Renee's belt free — the same hand, doing something else this time.

Trey and Kwame ran down a shopkeeper named Pham between two parked vans and argued about it for two streets before leaving him breathing outside a hospital. Later — though the two of them wouldn't know it yet, standing over him — that van would be opened again, and there would be two dozen people inside it who had been paid for, and Trey would drive them to the docks and give them what was in his pockets and tell them to go.

Clay was pulled from his own car by four officers who'd been told it was stolen, and it was Voss who walked into the middle of it and got him home. Clay returned the favor his own way — driving Trey, half a mile down the road, at a speed neither of them enjoyed, and then putting him out on the verge without a word.

Nadir waited outside Mateo's house that evening with the pistol in his coat. When Mateo came out, he raised it and shouted, and Rosie came off the porch at a run into her father's arms just as it went off. Nothing happened. The child was not marked, nor her father, and Nadir understood, later, why: it had already been decided, days earlier, at a counter with glass between him and the man who mocked him.

Voss picked up a hitchhiker in the rain, and a hand went into a pocket, and he fired twice and burned the car after. The detective sent to the ditch stopped over the body because he knew the shoes. His mother, on her kitchen floor, told him she'd asked him a hundred times to go and look.

Paula fell down her own stairs with no one home, and told the housekeeper in the ambulance that she was the best friend she had.

Snow came for the first time that winter, and two cars touched at a junction, and the shouting started before either driver had looked at the damage.

All night the helicopters went over, low and steady, spraying for the fruit fly, and every house in the city heard the same drone at the same hour: the Hartigans, dressing for a dinner party neither of them wanted; the Rennies, where a mother would soon leave for the club and a daughter would stay with her cello; the Rowe house, where a man cheating on his wife lay awake planning a lie involving a dog.

At the bakery, Otto Kemp took an order from a woman named Elaine — a cake, a name and an age on a card, ready Monday. Charlie Rill walked to school two days later and a waitress named Rhona, late for her shift, caught him with her wing mirror. He got up, said he was fine, refused a lift, and walked the rest of the way home insisting on it.

That night he did not wake properly. Grant and Elaine took up residence in a hospital chair, trading shifts, and into the corridor's silence came Duff, Grant's estranged father, with a coffee and, because he had nothing else to offer, a confession about a woman from decades ago. Grant said nothing back.

Nobody came for the cake. Nobody paid for it. Otto, bad at being ignored, began calling the Rill house at two in the morning to say the boy's name into the receiver.

Across town, Cheryl talked a man through his fantasy with the phone tucked under her chin while she folded nappies, and her husband Stu sat three feet away, saying nothing, getting worse. A week later he and Vern and two others walked into the mountains and found a young woman face down in the river. They tied a line to her ankle so she wouldn't drift and fished for two more days before telling anyone. When Vern told it at the table, wiping off his wife's clown makeup with a sponge, Iris stopped with the sponge still in her hand and looked at him like she'd never seen the face under his face either.

Vida sang six nights a week to a room that mostly talked through her, while at home her daughter Bee practiced cello alone. Meanwhile Rowe drove the family dog to the far side of the valley and left it there, to cover for the hours he'd spent with Nan; he told Peg it must have gotten over the fence. Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot — one of the very machines that had gone over the city that first night — heard she had someone new and spent an afternoon sawing her furniture into pieces.

House-sitting the Hartigans' place before the party, Ike and Dot made each other up as corpses and photographed themselves lying dead in the hall, laughing.

At the dinner itself, over the fish, Bess told Neil about the modelling session years ago, and then about the affair that came after it, and Neil set his glass down very carefully and made a scene in front of everyone.

Charlie died in the morning. That afternoon Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery to shout at the man who'd been calling them, and Otto sat them down and put warm bread in front of them, and it was Otto who learned, finally, whose birthday the cake had been for, and the three of them grieved together like strangers who had run out of anger.

Bee came home from rehearsal to find her mother asleep in the chair as always. She pulled the garage door down and started the car.

Not long after, at a picnic in the hills, a girl said something ordinary and wrong, and Stu picked up a rock and did what he had been carrying since the river.

Then the ground moved, eleven seconds of it, and by the evening bulletin all of it — the boy, the girl in the river, the girl in the hills, the wrecked furniture, the abandoned dog, the ruined dinner, the garage — had been folded into the same three minutes of news, as if none of it had ever needed telling apart.

Above the noise, at an open window, an old man was telling a younger one that nothing anybody does survives. "It isn't a complaint," he said. "It's just weather. You build the wall, the rain comes, the wall goes. Look down there if you don't believe me."

Two men were carried out through a crowd with their hands cuffed behind them — one shouting, one gone quiet in the particular way of someone who has already understood what he's done. Solly Two Coats and his crew walked into the diamond house dressed as pilgrims, heads bowed, and walked out with the finest stone the northern port had seen in a decade. By the time the alarm bells stopped ringing, they were gone.

Overseas, his cousin Marv got the news down a bad telephone line and gave one order: bring it straight over. No detours, no cleverness.

But cleverness was Solly's whole trade. In the city, Grigor the Nail steered him toward a bookmaker's shop to lay a bet on a fight — and, in the same breath, told the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno that the same shop was ripe for robbing. Neither party knew about the other.

Meanwhile, boxing men Halloway and Digby sent their fighter Pretty Sam to buy a caravan off a camp of travellers. Sam mouthed off to the wrong man. Finn, unlicensed and untested, knocked him cold in the dirt. That left Halloway with no fighter for Coldstone's fixed bout, so he threw Finn in instead and swore to Coldstone that the man would go down in the fourth.

Solly landed in the city, handed the stone to the fence Hersch for safekeeping, and carried an empty-looking case to the bookmaker's, meaning to place his bet in peace. Ike, Benno and their friend Tulley bungled the robbery there — grabbed Solly's arm and his case, and fled the shop with Grigor himself chasing them off, furious at the mess his own tip-off had made.

That night Finn ended the fixed fight in the first round, one punch, and Coldstone lost a fortune he took out of Halloway's hide with words alone — for now.

Marv, arriving to find no cousin and no stone, hired the bounty hunter Ledge, a man who tracked prizes by following whoever was clumsiest.

Grigor, holding the wrong man and the wrong case, cut off Solly's arm to force the lock and found nothing inside. The stone had never been in it.

Ledge, working faster, traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car apart, and took Ike, Benno, and the diamond they'd since dug out of hiding.

Coldstone fed what was left of Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby exactly what would happen to them if the second fight went the same way.

They told Finn to go down in the fourth again. Coldstone's men answered any doubt about their seriousness by burning Finn's mother alive in her caravan.

Grigor, still hunting the stone, ambushed Ledge's car with Ike and Benno inside. In the gunfire that followed, Ledge, Grigor and Benno were all left dead in the road, and the diamond lay loose among the wreckage.

Tulley, the last man standing from the botched robbery, slipped away — with the dog that had swallowed the stone before anyone could stop it.

At the rematch, Finn waited, obedient at last to the letter of the order, and dropped his man in the fourth round exactly as promised — while armed travellers moved through the crowd and cut down Coldstone's men one by one, repayment for the fire.

Halloway and Digby found Coldstone alone in the chaos and shot him where he stood. By morning the travellers had vanished from the camp as if they had never been there.

Weeks later, a stray dog was handed in at a pet shop, coughing and retching, and brought up a diamond onto the counter. It was Halloway and Digby, of all people, who stood there staring at it — the two men who had never robbed anyone, never chased anyone, holding the one thing that had cost so many others their lives.

The house was built for two and held five, plus the dog. Ruben slept on the couch, his mother kept the peace, and he watched Alma move through the kitchen with a hunger he told himself was patience. Nestor came home some nights with a scarf-smell of a chemist's shop still on him and knocked her into the counter for asking where the money went. Ruben started saying, quiet at first, that she should come away with him.

He'd noticed the dog kill things bigger than itself, and a neighbor told him what that was worth. Within a month Tigre was going into a pit twice a week and coming out every time, and Ruben was hiding the winnings for two people to leave on. Instead he paid two men in a bar to hurt his brother, thinking a hospital bed would slow him down. It didn't. Nestor worked out who'd sent them in a day, and left with Alma, the baby, and every note Ruben had hidden in the wardrobe.

Months later Nestor took a scarf and a gun into a bank and came out on the floor of it. At the funeral Ruben made his last offer, and Alma looked at him and said no, and meant it, and he understood then that she never would have come.

Before that, though — before the graveside — there had been the pit, and Chaco putting a pistol into Tigre's side when a fight went wrong, and Ruben going over the rope with a knife, and running with Pipo into the truck, and driving it through a red light into a small car turning across the junction, the dog bleeding out across the back seat.

Celine had not been thinking about junctions that morning. She'd moved into Hector's new flat months before, after he walked out of a birthday party on a wife and two daughters, and the flat had a window facing her own face forty feet tall on a hoarding across the street. She was still getting used to living across from herself when the car spun and stopped and the world went white.

She woke in a hospital with a cage of steel through her leg and asked first about Chispa, who'd been alone in the flat and hadn't been seen since. The little dog had gone through a gap in the boards and couldn't climb back, and her whining came up through every room. Hector took up the floor plank by plank with a crowbar while Celine's leg went from ache to something the nurses wouldn't say the name of. It went above the knee in the end. The same week, men came and stripped the hoarding and pasted something else over her face, and the two of them sat in the wrecked flat looking at a blank frame where she used to be.

At the junction itself, before any of that, a vagrant with a cart of scrap had stood in the smoke and simply lifted the bleeding dog out of the back seat and walked off with it, while everyone else ran toward the wrecks. His name was Cardo. He nursed the dog for weeks in a yard full of strays, feeding it by hand, until it slept against him and followed him into the street each morning.

A man named Elian met him behind a church and paid him to kill his own half-brother Sergio. Cardo took the advance, took Sergio off a pavement, and instead of killing him chained him to a bed frame among the empty kennels. He'd already stood a long way back at his own wife's burial that year, among people who thought he'd died decades before, and followed his grown daughter Perla home through three streets without speaking to her.

He came back one evening to a yard of dead dogs and Tigre standing among them with its muzzle wet, put the gun to its head, and could not fire. He brought Elian face to face with Sergio, left a loaded pistol on the floor between them, and walked out with money from both. Then he let himself into Perla's flat while she was at work, sat an hour on her bed, and told an answering machine everything he'd never said to her face, taking one photograph on his way out.

Shaved, in clothes that didn't fit, he left his money on her table and walked out into the wasteland at the city's edge with the dog beside him, the ground flat and grey and going nowhere in particular.

Emlyn came to Wilder's house that same evening, still in his coat, and sat down as if he had been summoned to discuss a manuscript rather than a marriage. "I've known for four years," he said. "Since the trip abroad. She told me herself, in the hotel, after you were foolish enough to write to her there. I read the letters too, before I gave them back to her. I never thought much of your prose style, if it's any comfort."

It was not the confession Wilder had braced for. He had rung in a state, expecting to be the one delivering news, and instead found the news already old, already digested, already turned into something Emlyn could hand back to him like a returned proof.

That state had begun an hour earlier, over drinks with Odile in a bar, when she had let slip, almost carelessly, that Emlyn was publishing a writer Wilder represented — a man both of them privately despised — and Wilder had understood all at once that the two men's lives had gone on touching each other in rooms he knew nothing about. He'd rung Emlyn before he had time to decide whether he wanted to.

Odile herself had come to that bar to say her marriage was over, that she had spent the night before confessing everything to her husband, at last, completely, as though it were the first time such a thing had happened. She said it with the relief of a woman putting down a weight she had carried alone. She did not know — could not have known, from the way Wilder's face changed — that she was two years late in thinking herself unburdened.

Those two years had begun in the rented rooms, when the linen and the crockery that had once made the affair feel like a second, sustainable life had come to seem instead like duties, like another marriage to maintain. They split the plates between them without much ceremony and gave up the lease, not because anyone had found them out, but because the rooms had stopped feeling like anything at all.

Before that came the dinners at Emlyn and Odile's own table, where the two men talked racquets and schoolboy games with an ease that left her no part in the conversation, an intimacy she could not enter no matter how long she sat there. And before that, the long lunch at which Emlyn baited Wilder about contemporary fiction for hours, drink after drink, never once saying the thing Wilder didn't yet know he knew — Odile's confession sitting behind every word like a held breath.

And before that: Odile going back to the rented rooms and saying nothing of the trip, letting the afternoon pass exactly as all the others had, so that Wilder went on in ignorance while she carried, alone, the knowledge that Emlyn now knew.

And before that: the hotel abroad, the letter waiting at the desk in a hand Emlyn recognised, his quiet question about it, and her confession following almost at once — met not with anger but with Emlyn's strange, level remark that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife.

And before all of it, further back than any of them now cared to measure exactly: Odile telling Wilder she was carrying her husband's child, and the two of them deciding, in the rooms they'd made their own, that nothing between them needed to change. Before that, the household itself — the linen, the plates, the ordinary objects that had made betrayal feel like domestic life. And before that, the beginning of all of it: a party at Emlyn's house, Wilder leading Odile upstairs while the other guests drank below, and telling her, with the guests' laughter rising faintly through the floor, how lovely she was.

Emlyn sat now with his coat still on, waiting for Wilder to say something worth the years of silence, and finding, when nothing came, that he had already said everything himself.

Listen: he has already been shot, and he is being born, and he is standing on the radio explaining the fourth dimension, and all of this is happening now, because that is the only tense the aliens ever taught him to use.

He is a weak, peculiar child in a small industrial town. His father throws him into the deep end of a pool to teach him to swim, and he sinks, and at the bottom he finds that he does not especially want to come up. This is not a memory he tells in order. It arrives the way all his memories arrive, unstuck, adjacent to whatever else is happening in his skull at the time.

On another day, which is also this day, he is old, addressing a crowd about the death he has always known would come to him, and a beam weapon ends the lecture exactly as he predicted, and the audience understands, too late, that a man who says he knows the hour of his own death is not always merely eccentric.

He is drafted as a chaplain's assistant, shipped overseas with no training worth the name, and lost behind enemy lines with a scout who beats him for asking to be left in a ditch to die. They are captured together. The scout dies of gangrene on the packed prison train, and with his last breath he says the boy's name like a curse, blaming him for everything that has happened to both of them. Somewhere in the same period — before, after, it hardly matters to the telling — a fellow prisoner hears the dead man's grievance and promises, quietly, patiently, that the debt will be collected. Years later. In its own time. This promise sits in the story like a stone dropped in dark water: you hear it long before you see where it lands.

He is housed with other prisoners beside enemy officers who have, through some clerical error, been drawing double rations for years, plump and prosperous in captivity while the new arrivals starve. He is moved on to a great city and lodged in a disused abattoir, in a meat locker with a number over the door. The city burns in a single night. He and the others come up from the cellar to find it erased — streets, buildings, the neighbors who fed them, all of it ash. They are made to dig bodies out of ruined cellars until one of the diggers dies of nothing but the dry heaves, retching himself to death over what he has to touch.

He comes home. He collapses. In the hospital a fellow patient hands him paperback novels by a hack science fiction writer, and something in their impossible physics fits the shape of what he cannot otherwise say about the war.

He marries the daughter of a man who owns an optometry school, and becomes rich, and this prosperity sits in the account like a fact awaiting its undoing. He survives a plane crash in the mountains. His wife, driving to see him in the hospital, dies of exhaust fumes in her own car — the least dramatic death in the story, arriving with no more weight than a comma.

He says he was taken by aliens after that, kept in a zoo on their planet alongside a film actress, their intimacy studied like weather. The aliens tell him that every moment that ever was or will be exists all at once, that his idea of choosing anything is a parochial embarrassment particular to his species. He believes this completely, or says he does, and it is impossible now to tell if the zoo caused the belief or the belief caused the zoo.

He goes on the radio to explain the fourth dimension to strangers. His daughter, hearing this, decides her father is senile and quietly takes his affairs out of his hands, meaning to protect him from himself.

And then the lecture hall, and the beam weapon, and the audience, and the old promise from the prison train finally collected on schedule, though no one watching could have said which of all these mornings came first, or whether, from where he was standing, any of them did.

Somewhere in the same period — before, after, it hardly matters to the telling — a fellow prisoner hears the dead man's grievance and promises, quietly, patiently, that the debt will be collected. Years later. In its own time. This promise sits in the story like a stone dropped in dark water: you hear it long before you see where it lands.

He is housed with other prisoners beside enemy officers who have, through some clerical error, been drawing double rations for years, plump and prosperous in captivity while the new arrivals starve. He is moved on to a great city and lodged in a disused abattoir, in a meat locker with a number over the door. The city burns in a single night. He and the others come up from the cellar to find it erased — streets, buildings, the neighbors who fed them, all of it ash. They are made to dig bodies out of ruined cellars until one of the diggers dies of nothing but the dry heaves, retching himself to death over what he has to touch.

He comes home. He collapses. In the hospital a fellow patient hands him paperback novels by a hack science fiction writer, and something in their impossible physics fits the shape of what he cannot otherwise say about the war.

He marries the daughter of a man who owns an optometry school, and becomes rich, and this prosperity sits in the account like a fact awaiting its undoing. He survives a plane crash in the mountains. His wife, driving to see him in the hospital, dies of exhaust fumes in her own car — the least dramatic death in the story, arriving with no more weight than a comma.

He says he was taken by aliens after that, kept in a zoo on their planet alongside a film actress, their intimacy studied like weather. The aliens tell him that every moment that ever was or will be exists all at once, that his idea of choosing anything is a parochial embarrassment particular to his species. He believes this completely, or says he does, and it is impossible now to tell if the zoo caused the belief or the belief caused the zoo.

He goes on the radio to explain the fourth dimension to strangers. His daughter, hearing this, decides her father is senile and quietly takes his affairs out of his hands, meaning to protect him from himself.

And then the lecture hall, and the beam weapon, and the audience, and the old promise from the prison train finally collected on schedule, though no one watching could have said which of all these mornings came first, or whether, from where he was standing, any of them did.
